strengths: Elegant and computationally efficient formulation: The proposed stochastic FIM estimator using Hutchinson's trick combined with detached probabilities (Eq. 2) enables an unbiased rank-1 estimate of the exact Fisher Information Matrix (and its diagonal/trace) in a single backward pass, avoiding the need to loop over classes or sample labels.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The paper provides clear, solid proofs characterizing the spectrum of the simplex core FIM, establishing Loewner order envelopes, and deriving sharp deterministic bounds on the neuromanifold FIM.

Bounded relative variance: The variance analysis rigorously shows that the coefficient of variation (CV) of the Hutchinson estimator's diagonal elements is bounded by $\sqrt{2}$, in contrast to standard Monte Carlo Fisher estimators whose CV can diverge.

Clear exposition: The paper is well-organized, with a clean flow from the geometry of the low-dimensional core space to the high-dimensional neuromanifold, followed by stochastic estimators and proofs.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates the estimator only via static density plots of diagonal FIM values on 128 samples of DistilBERT. Demonstrating practical utility in downstream tasks—such as natural gradient descent / second-order optimization, Laplace approximations, continual learning (EWC), or network pruning—would dramatically strengthen the work.

Missing empirical benchmarking of computational efficiency and variance: There are no runtime or wall-clock comparisons against standard baselines (e.g., standard Monte Carlo Fisher sampling, BackPACK-style exact diagonal Fisher, or empirical Fisher), nor is there an empirical study validating the variance reduction rate as a function of the number of random probes.

Practicality of the low-rank core estimator ($h^{\text{LR}}$): The low-rank bound estimator requires running power iterations per sample to compute the top eigenvector $v_C$ and eigenvalue $\lambda_C$. Given that the primary Hutchinson estimator $h$ already requires only one backward pass without iterative eigensolvers, the practical motivation for computing $h^{\text{LR}}$ in deep learning pipelines is less clear.

strengths: The paper introduces a mathematically elegant formulation (Eq. 2) that allows an unbiased stochastic estimate of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) via a single backward pass, combining Hutchinson-style random probes with detached square-root class probabilities.

The theoretical characterization of the estimator's variance is solid, demonstrating that the coefficient of variation (CV) for the diagonal entries is bounded by $\sqrt{2}$, which avoids the heavy-tailed variance issues of naive Monte Carlo label sampling.

The analysis of the 'core space' (the statistical simplex for categorical outputs) provides rigorous Löwner ordering bounds and spectral characterizations that propagate systematically to the high-dimensional neuromanifold.
weaknesses: The practical value of the proposed estimator remains unvalidated in actual machine learning workflows. While natural gradient optimization, curvature regularization, and Laplace approximations are heavily cited as motivations, the paper does not evaluate the estimator in any downstream task (such as training a model with a natural gradient optimizer, continual learning/EWC, or uncertainty quantification).

The empirical evaluation is extremely thin, consisting solely of kernel density estimates of diagonal entries computed on 128 samples using DistilBERT on AG News and SST-2. This serves as little more than a sanity check and does not benchmark wall-clock overhead, convergence rates, or memory trade-offs against established baselines (e.g., K-FAC, BackPACK, empirical Fisher, or Monte Carlo Fisher).

The theoretical results concerning the simplex FIM $\mathcal{I}^\Delta(z) = \text{diag}(p) - pp^\top$ largely rely on standard rank-1 perturbation theory and Cauchy interlacing, offering modest conceptual novelty to the information geometry literature.

The worst-case bounds on the empirical Fisher (Lemma 4 and Proposition 11) assume an adversarially chosen label $y$, which is disconnected from realistic supervised learning scenarios where labels are drawn from the data distribution.

strengths: Elegant formulation of Hutchinson's estimator for the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM): by introducing the detached square-root probability scalar function in Eq. (2), the method computes an unbiased rank-1 sample of the true expected FIM using a single backward pass without needing per-class backpropagation.

Solid theoretical characterization of the core simplex FIM spectrum (Theorem 1) and Löwner order bounds (Lemma 2), which cleanly translate into deterministic bounds on the neuromanifold FIM (Propositions 6-9).

Rigorous variance analysis: the authors prove that the element-wise variance of the diagonal Hutchinson estimator yields a bounded coefficient of variation (bounded by sqrt(2)), contrasting sharply with standard Monte Carlo sampling which can exhibit unbounded CV under heavy-tailed activations/inputs.
weaknesses: Severely limited empirical evaluation: the empirical section is restricted to static kernel density plots of diagonal FIM values evaluated on only 128 samples of DistilBERT for two classification datasets (AG News and SST-2).

No downstream validation: the paper does not demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed estimator in any standard FIM application, such as natural gradient optimization, K-FAC/preconditioned training, Laplace approximation, continual learning, or model pruning.

Lack of scalability analysis for large output spaces: Eq. (2) requires summing over all classes C. While practical for small C (e.g., C=2 or 4 as tested), the approach becomes computationally expensive or memory-heavy for large vocabulary sizes (e.g., language modeling where C is 32k-100k+), a limitation that is not discussed or evaluated against standard Monte Carlo label sampling.

Practical implications of the rank-1 property: each Hutchinson sample produces a rank-1 matrix. The paper does not systematically study how many samples or what moving average schedules are required to obtain stable preconditioning matrices in actual training settings.

strengths: The paper provides an elegant and insightful connection between the low-dimensional geometry of the statistical simplex (the 'core space') and the high-dimensional neuromanifold, deriving clean spectral characterizations and Löwner-order bounds.

The proposed Hutchinson-based stochastic FIM estimator is technically clever and practically convenient: by weighting the log-likelihood with detached square-root probabilities and random probes, it allows computing an unbiased estimate of the FIM using only a single backward pass.
Theoretical guarantees on the variance of the estimator are solid, showing that the coefficient of variation of diagonal entries is rigorously bounded by $\sqrt{2}$ for Rademacher probes.

The empirical evaluation is thorough in comparing the estimated diagonal Fisher information against the exact ground truth across multiple architectures (Transformers, CNNs, audio models) and modalities, confirming significant accuracy improvements over empirical Fisher.
weaknesses: The paper evaluates the estimator purely in terms of matrix entry estimation accuracy (RelMAE) on frozen models, but does not demonstrate downstream impact in actual applications such as natural gradient descent, model pruning, or Laplace approximations.

The rank-1 nature of a single probe realization means that for curvature-based optimization or non-diagonal approximations, many probes or exponential moving averages are needed; empirical analysis of how moving averages behave during dynamic training is missing.
The paper exceeds standard conference length (12 pages of main text before references/appendix), which may require substantial condensing for typical 8–9 page limits.

strengths: Novel and elegant algorithmic trick: The introduction of the scalar function h(D_x, theta) using detached probabilities and random Rademacher/Gaussian probes enables unbiased estimation of the full Fisher Information Matrix (and its diagonal) in a single backward pass, circumventing the need for multiple class/sample-wise backpropagations.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The paper establishes thorough spectral bounds and envelope properties of the simplex FIM ('core space') and successfully lifts them to the parameter manifold via the parameter-output Jacobian, including tightness and norm error bounds.

Bounded variance guarantees: Unlike naive Monte Carlo estimators whose coefficient of variation can be unbounded under heavy-tailed features, Proposition 11 and its proofs formally prove that the Hutchinson estimator has a coefficient of variation strictly bounded by sqrt(2).

Diverse empirical validation of estimation accuracy: Experiments cover a wide range of architectures (transformer, CNN, speech models) across NLP, vision, and audio, explicitly verifying estimation error (RelMAE) against true closed-form diagonal FIM values.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream application validation: While the estimator is shown to accurately approximate the true diagonal FIM, the paper does not demonstrate empirical improvements in downstream tasks that rely on the FIM, such as natural gradient optimization, Laplace approximations, network pruning, or continual learning.

Rank-1 limitation per step: Each draw of the Hutchinson estimator produces a rank-1 matrix; while its expectation equals the true FIM and the diagonal is readily extracted, practical usage for full or block-structured preconditioning requires moving averages or multiple probes, which is discussed but not thoroughly explored experimentally.

Theoretical critique of MC estimators in Section 4.1 is somewhat idealized: The toy example relies on an unbounded fourth moment / heavy-tailed input distribution, which, while theoretically valid, does not necessarily reflect standard normalized deep learning datasets.

Clarity and motivation of some deterministic bounds: Some of the Löwner and Frobenius norm bounds in Section 3, while mathematically sound, are dense and not directly linked to the design or improvement of the stochastic estimators introduced in Section 4.

strengths: The paper introduces an unbiased stochastic estimator for the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and its diagonal/trace that can be computed via a single backward pass by defining an auxiliary scalar objective with random Rademacher/Gaussian probes.
The theoretical variance of the diagonal entries of the estimator w.r.t. the random probe is rigorously derived (Proposition 11), demonstrating a coefficient of variation bounded by sqrt(2).

The paper provides a detailed spectral characterization of the categorical Fisher information matrix on the probability simplex (the 'core space') and uses it to construct deterministic Loewner-order bounds and trace bounds for the neuromanifold FIM.

The experimental evaluation covers a diverse set of architectures and modalities (DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, Wav2Vec2) across NLP, vision, and audio tasks to verify the numerical accuracy of diagonal FIM estimation.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch in the critique of Monte Carlo (MC) estimators: Section 4.1 argues that MC estimators suffer from unbounded variance due to heavy-tailed input distributions p(x). However, the variance bound in Proposition 11 is computed strictly conditionally on a fixed dataset D_x with respect to the probe xi. If minibatches are sampled from a heavy-tailed data distribution, the proposed estimator inherits the exact same variance w.r.t. p(x). Conversely, for a fixed batch D_x, the categorical distribution p(y|x) has finite support {1, ..., C} and cannot produce heavy tails.

Exclusion of the natural single-pass MC baseline: The paper states that the MC estimate is excluded because 'it requires B backward passes per batch'. This is inaccurate. By applying a batch-level Rademacher vector to the sampled per-example losses (i.e., backpropagating through sum_x xi_x ell_{x, y_hat_x} with y_hat_x ~ p(y|x)), an unbiased MC estimate of the diagonal FIM can also be obtained in a single backward pass. Failing to compare against this stochastic MC probe baseline leaves the empirical evaluation incomplete.

Limited theoretical novelty in the core space bounds: The simplex FIM is the classical covariance matrix of a multinomial distribution, diag(p) - pp^T. The spectral properties and Loewner bounds in Section 2 and Section 3 largely represent direct applications of standard matrix analysis (Cauchy interlacing theorem for rank-one perturbations of diagonal matrices, Gershgorin circle theorem, and Loewner order preservation under congruence transformations).

Scalability constraints for large label/output spaces: The proposed estimator requires instantiating and backpropagating through probes of dimension |D_x| * C. While practical for small classification tasks (C <= 100), this poses substantial memory and compute bottlenecks for large label spaces (e.g., language modeling with vocabulary size V >= 32,000 across sequence lengths).

Lack of downstream task evaluation: The empirical evaluation is restricted to computing relative mean absolute error (RelMAE) on a static set of 128 batches. The paper does not demonstrate whether the improved diagonal estimation translates to measurable performance gains in downstream applications where the FIM is used, such as natural gradient optimization, Laplace approximations, or neural network pruning.
